title: Al-Malik, the King
hookLine: the King, whose kingdom never ends, and everything in your hands on loan from it
tomorrow: a King with no flaw at all. what does 'pure' even mean?

cards: The lease, the car title, the account in your name: paperwork says who owns what. Yesterday ended on a question: if mercy is that close, who's actually in charge here? The Qur'an answers with the third name.
Al-Malik, the King. Surah al-Mulk opens, in Pickthall's words: Blessed is He in Whose hand is the Sovereignty.

teach.b: Al-Malik comes from the root m-l-k: to own, to rule. Surah Al Imran gives a line to say about it, beginning, in Pickthall's words: Say: O Allah!
Owner of Sovereignty! The verse goes on: You give sovereignty to whom You will, and You take it from whom You will. Every crown is on loan, and so is every key on your ring.
In the Qur'an, Pharaoh is the king who forgot it, announcing to his people that he was their highest lord. That doesn't make things cheap.
A borrowed thing is treated with more care, not less; it just isn't gripped. And that's this week, too, held in an open hand. The forty as a life.
One, by heart. Pass one on. Every name a door.
Mercy for all. Mercy for me.
Six things gathered, none of them owned, all of them lent to carry.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the Qur'an's word for a kingdom, mulk, comes from the same root as the word for owning.

how: At a loss, Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, we belong to Allah and to Him we return, and many think of what they hold as a trust from Him.

o: the One who judges every deed done
a title for a scholar who leads a school
the King, who owns and rules all

p: in Whose hand is the Sovereignty

s: if everything is on loan, things don't really matter
a borrowed thing is treated with more care, not less; it just isn't gripped.
Surah al-Mulk opens by blessing the One in whose hand is the Sovereignty
Pickthall: Blessed is He in Whose hand is the Sovereignty.
the Qur'an says sovereignty is given and taken by Allah
Owner of Sovereignty: You give it to whom You will, and take it from whom You will.

games.q: a friend lends you her laptop for a week while yours is in the shop. it's older than yours and a bit slow. what does Al-Malik say about how you treat it?
o: with care; what's lent is handled carefully, never treated as yours.
it's old anyway, so a few scratches won't matter much.
it's all on loan from Allah, so it's not worth worrying about.
games.why: if everything is on loan, a borrowed thing gets more care, not less. that's how the name loosens the grip without making things cheap.

practice: Hold something you own on your open palm: keys, a ring, your phone. Don't grip it; let it rest there, flat. For the sit, keep the hand open, holding it the way you'd hold something lent.

wordCard.voice: Al-Malik: the King, the Owner of sovereignty, whose kingdom never ends.

orig.note: Arabic: the King, from m-l-k, to own and to rule.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: his kingdom, and everything in my hands on loan from it. That's a week of names begun.
